query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in the eutectic HEA is driven by differential oxidation and spallation of phase‐specific oxide films, where the mechanically unstable, less-adherent oxides on certain phases (e.g., B2 or hard phase) are repeatedly removed by sliding wear while relatively more protective oxides on soft (fcc) phases only partially recover, leading to cyclic breakdown and local corrosion acceleration.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a finely lamellar architecture featuring alternating soft (fcc) and hard (B2/bcc) phases that develop distinct oxide scales upon high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion in a high-temperature, chloride-containing acidic or saline environment, and compare with controls under static corrosion or wear-only conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (600–800 °C) in a corrosive medium where oxide films can form, yet are continuously disrupted by imposed reciprocating sliding wear under controlled load and speed.
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase boundaries and differences in oxide adhesion properties dictated by the eutectic phases’ composition.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperature, each phase forms its own oxide: the softer fcc phase tends to form a relatively protective, adherent oxide, while the harder B2/bcc phase forms a less-stable oxide. Under sliding wear, localized mechanical stresses preferentially spall the less-adherent oxide, exposing fresh metal that oxidizes rapidly but without uniform healing. This differential oxide formation and repeated mechanical removal create a positive feedback loop where wear accelerates corrosion and vice versa.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to corrosion-only tests, the simultaneous wear-corrosion condition will yield significantly thinner, patchy oxide films (with measurable differences between phases), higher localized corrosion pit densities, and deeper, more extensive wear scars along phase boundaries, with both individual wear rates and corrosion current densities substantially elevated.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEA samples subjected to static high-temperature corrosion (allowing full oxide growth) or wear-only experiments in inert media.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies when the oxide films have the capacity to form initially but lack self-healing under high cyclic mechanical stress; if test conditions (such as lower wear intensity or an environment that promotes continuous oxide repair) prevail, the degradation rate may not be accelerated.
generation.uncertainty: While the conceptual framework is supported by known oxidation kinetics and wear mechanics, the precise quantitative relationships between mechanical stress, oxide thickness variations on each phase, and corrosion kinetics require further time-resolved studies using high-temperature microscopy and surface analyses. The possibility of partial self-healing under specific conditions introduces additional nuance, but the primary mechanism remains oxide spallation-induced acceleration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one subjected to simultaneous wear-corrosion at elevated temperature and one under static corrosion-only conditions. Use in-situ high-temperature microscopy and post-test SEM/EDS to monitor oxide film integrity and phase-specific oxide thickness.
measurements: Time-resolved measurement of oxide thickness and spallation frequency on each phase.
Profilometry to quantify wear depth and corrosion pit density.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy before and after tests to assess passive film quality.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneous wear condition does not result in significantly thinner or more disrupted oxide films, nor in higher localized corrosion (i.e., if oxide film characteristics and degradation rates are statistically equivalent to static corrosion), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTThe ongoing demand for high‐thrust turbine engines necessitates the advance of next‐generation structural materials capable of withstanding higher temperatures. Commercial MCrAlY alloy, used as bond coats crucial for thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems, face a fundamental temperature ceiling of ∼1100 °C due to accelerated oxidation and spallation. Here, we design a novel Y and Hf co‐doped NiCoCrAl‐type multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) that achieves exceptional 1200 °C oxidation resistance primarily through lattice distortion‐induced diffusion suppression. Compared with typical NiCoCrAlY alloy, the MPEA exhibits 59% lower in thermally grown oxide (TGO) growth rate, as well as negligible TGO spallation after 500 h at 1200°C. This performance stems from a significantly refined eutectic structure enabling rapid formation of a protective Al2O3 scale during initial oxidation, coupled with lattice distortion that elevates vacancy formation energy and Al migration barriers within the Al‐depletion zone (ADZ), drastically reducing sustained diffusion rates. This co‐design strategy, integrating tailored microstructure and lattice distortion, establishes a new paradigm for ultra‐

In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.
